related_questions.question: Does celiac disease ever go away?

text_blocks.snippet: No, celiac disease does not go away. It is a lifelong autoimmune condition. While a strict gluten-free diet can manage symptoms and allow the small intestine to heal, the disease itself remains, according to health organizations. If gluten is reintroduced, the immune system will react, causing damage to the small intestine and triggering symptoms again, says the Celiac Disease Foundation.

related_questions.snippet: Celiac disease causes damage to the small intestine. This makes it hard for the body to absorb vitamins and other nutrients. You cannot prevent celiac disease. But you can stop and reverse the damage to the small intestine by eating a strict gluten-free diet.

related_questions.question: Is it possible to cure celiac disease?

text_blocks.snippet: No, celiac disease cannot be cured. However, a gluten-free diet can effectively manage symptoms and allow the small intestine to heal. While the disease itself is not curable, avoiding gluten is the primary treatment and allows individuals with celiac disease to live a healthy life.
snippet_highlighted_words: No, celiac disease cannot be cured

list.title: Gluten-free diet is the only established treatment:
list.snippet: A lifelong gluten-free diet is the cornerstone of managing celiac disease. This diet eliminates gluten, a protein found in wheat, barley, and rye, which triggers the autoimmune response in individuals with celiac disease.

list.title: Intestinal Healing:
list.snippet: When gluten is removed from the diet, the inflammation in the small intestine subsides, and the villi (tiny, finger-like projections that absorb nutrients) begin to heal and regain their ability to absorb nutrients effectively.

list.title: No permanent damage:
list.snippet: The villi are not permanently damaged and will heal with a gluten-free diet.

list.title: Ongoing research:
list.snippet: While a gluten-free diet remains the primary treatment, research is ongoing to find other therapies that may complement or potentially replace it, such as immunotherapies and drugs that target specific aspects of the immune response.

list.title: Preventing complications:
list.snippet: A gluten-free diet helps prevent long-term complications associated with untreated celiac disease, such as anemia, osteoporosis, and an increased risk of certain cancers.

text_blocks.snippet: In essence, while a cure for celiac disease is not yet available, a gluten-free diet is highly effective in managing the condition and allowing individuals to live a symptom-free and healthy life, according to the Celiac Disease Foundation.

related_questions.question: What happens if you keep eating gluten with celiac disease?

text_blocks.snippet: If someone with celiac disease continues to eat gluten, it triggers an immune response that damages the small intestine, leading to malabsorption of nutrients and various health complications. Even without noticeable symptoms, ongoing gluten consumption can lead to long-term health issues like anemia, osteoporosis, and an increased risk of certain cancers according to the Celiac Disease Foundation.
snippet_highlighted_words: it triggers an immune response that damages the small intestine, leading to malabsorption of nutrients and various health complications

list.title: Intestinal Damage:
list.snippet: The primary issue is the damage to the small intestine's lining, which impairs its ability to absorb nutrients properly.

list.title: Malabsorption:
list.snippet: This damage leads to malabsorption, where the body doesn't get the necessary vitamins and minerals from food, potentially causing deficiencies.

list.title: Anemia:
list.snippet: Iron deficiency anemia can result from poor iron absorption, leading to fatigue and shortness of breath.

list.title: Bone Health Issues:
list.snippet: Calcium deficiency due to malabsorption can weaken bones, potentially leading to osteopenia (low bone density) or osteoporosis.

list.title: Increased Cancer Risk:
list.snippet: Long-term, unmanaged celiac disease can increase the risk of certain cancers.

list.title: Other Complications:
list.snippet: Celiac disease can also manifest as dermatitis herpetiformis (a skin condition), neurological problems, and other issues.

list.title: Symptoms:
list.snippet: While some individuals may not experience noticeable symptoms, others may have digestive issues like diarrhea, bloating, and stomach pain, or more general symptoms like fatigue and weight loss.
